rationale: Both preserve the bruised reed and smoldering wick and connect this restraint with judgment. Isaiah says judgment in truth; Matthew says justice brought forth to victory.

relationship: explicit quotation of the nations hoping in the servant's name
rationale: Matthew concludes its servant citation with nations hoping in His name, matching the source's final clause. It does not repeat this unit's promise that he will shine forth and not be broken.

relationship: close Creator giving life and breath to humanity
rationale: Isaiah identifies God as maker of heaven, earth and its contents and giver of breath to its people; Paul likewise names the Maker of the world and Lord of heaven and earth who gives everyone life and breath.

relationship: internal appointment as covenant and light for nations
rationale: Both describe God's servant appointed as a covenant for a people or race and a light for nations. Isaiah 49 additionally spells out restoration of Israel's dispersion and salvation to earth's extremity.

relationship: related light-for-nations image applied to Jesus
rationale: Isaiah appoints the servant a light for nations; Simeon, holding Jesus, calls the salvation he has seen a light for revelation to nations and glory for Israel. Luke's setting gives the image a specified application.

relationship: related mission of opening blind eyes and releasing captives
rationale: Isaiah joins sight for blind people with release from bonds and prison darkness; Jesus reads a mission of recovery of sight and release for captives and the oppressed. Luke's cited passage shares these motifs without being presented as a verbatim quotation of this unit.

relationship: internal refusal to give God's glory to another
rationale: Both directly state that God will not give His glory to another. Isaiah 42 additionally says He will not give His praiseworthy deeds to carved images, while Isaiah 48 connects the declaration with His profaned name.

relationship: internal announcement preceding fulfillment
rationale: Isaiah 42 distinguishes former things arrived from new things disclosed before appearing; Isaiah 48 likewise says God announced former events before acting and before they arrived, preventing their attribution to idols.

relationship: close new song and praise extending across the earth
rationale: Both summon a new song to the Lord and proclamation of His name and glory across the earth and peoples. Isaiah specifically includes seafarers, islands and their inhabitants.

relationship: internal summons for the wilderness to rejoice
rationale: Both directly summon wilderness or desert places to rejoicing. Isaiah 42 names Kedar and Petra and their inhabitants; Isaiah 35 describes flowering desert places and the sight of God's glory.

relationship: parallel giving of glory to God among peoples
rationale: Isaiah predicts giving God glory and announcing His praiseworthy deeds in the islands; the psalm commands families of nations to bring the Lord glory and honor for His name.

relationship: close Lord shattering war and enemies
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord will crush war and cry mightily against His enemies; Exodus calls Him the One who shatters wars and praises His right hand shattering enemies. The supplied wording concerns His breaking war, not a substituted warrior title.

relationship: parallel divine silence ending in intervention
rationale: Isaiah's God says He was silent but will not remain silent and hold back; the psalm likewise moves from God's silence while wrongdoing continued to His announced rebuke. Isaiah's childbirth and drying imagery is additional.

relationship: related transformation of waters into dry territory
rationale: Isaiah turns rivers into islands and dries marshes; the psalm turns rivers into wilderness and water outlets into thirst. Both describe divine removal or transformation of watery places, with different resulting terrain.

relationship: related opening of sight and movement from darkness to light
rationale: Isaiah promises guidance for blind people and darkness turned to light; Jesus commissions Paul to open people's eyes so they turn from darkness to light and from Satan's authority to God. Acts explicitly describes conversion, while Isaiah also supplies road imagery.

relationship: close shame of those trusting and worshiping images
rationale: Isaiah commands shame upon those trusting carved images and calling cast images their gods; the psalm likewise calls those bowing to carved images and boasting in idols to shame.

relationship: parallel call for unresponsive people to hear
rationale: Isaiah commands deaf people to listen and blind people to look and see; Jeremiah summons Jacob and Judah to hear while describing people with eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear.

relationship: related failure of spiritual perception among a people and its guides
rationale: Isaiah rebukes blind servants of God and deaf rulers; Jesus calls the Pharisees blind guides of blind people. The sensory diagnoses and groups differ, while both expose failed religious perception.

relationship: close rebuke for seeing and hearing without understanding
rationale: Isaiah says the hearers saw but did not keep watch and had opened ears but did not listen; Jesus asks His disciples why their eyes and ears do not perceive and why they do not understand.

relationship: related vindication of God amid human unfaithfulness
rationale: Isaiah says the Lord wished to be justified and magnify praise; Paul defends God's faithfulness and applies the saying that God is justified in His words. The comparison concerns divine vindication, preserving the source's actual praise language.

relationship: parallel people becoming plunder without rescuing care
rationale: Isaiah describes people plundered with no rescuer or demand for their return; Ezekiel describes God's sheep plundered because their shepherds failed to seek them, followed by God's promised rescue. The flock image is Ezekiel's particular formulation.

relationship: parallel God handing disobedient Israel to plunderers
rationale: Isaiah identifies God as the One who gave Jacob and Israel to plunder because they sinned and refused His ways; Judges likewise records Israel forsaking Him and His handing them to plunderers and enemies.

relationship: parallel severe judgment without the required response
rationale: Isaiah describes war and surrounding burning without understanding or taking it to heart; Amos describes sword, camps in fire and a firebrand rescued from burning, yet no return to God. The absent responses are expressed differently.

relationship: related belonging expressed through calling by name
rationale: God calls Israel by name and claims it as His own; Jesus' shepherd figure calls his own sheep by name and leads them. The collective address and the individual sheep in the figure differ.

relationship: historical counterpart to safe passage through water
rationale: Isaiah promises God's presence and protection when His people cross waters; Exodus records the Lord opening the sea and Israel walking within it on dry ground between walls of water.

relationship: narrative counterpart to unharmed presence amid fire
rationale: Isaiah promises that flame will not burn the people passing through fire; Daniel describes the Lord's angel joining the companions in the furnace and the fire neither touching nor distressing them.

relationship: related Egypt given as divine compensation
rationale: Isaiah names Egypt as an exchange on Israel's behalf; Ezekiel describes God giving Egypt to Babylon's king as wages in exchange for service against Tyre. Recipients and grounds differ, and Ezekiel does not supply Isaiah's Ethiopia and Soene clauses.

relationship: related another person given in place of a favored recipient
rationale: Isaiah promises people and rulers on Israel's behalf; Proverbs describes the righteous escaping a hunt and the impious handed over in his place. Proverbs specifies moral categories that Isaiah does not assign to the exchanged rulers.

relationship: close gathering of the redeemed from east and west
rationale: Isaiah promises to bring offspring from the east and gather the people from the west; the psalm calls the redeemed to thanksgiving and says God gathered them from countries including east and west, with north and sea also named.

relationship: internal return of sons and daughters from abroad
rationale: Isaiah 43 commands distant regions to bring God's sons and daughters; Isaiah 49 describes a signal to nations and islands followed by sons brought in the bosom and daughters carried on shoulders. The manner of their return is developed differently.

relationship: related community bearing God's name
rationale: Isaiah includes all called by God's name in the gathering of His formed people; Jeremiah's community appeals to the fact that God's name has been called over them and asks Him not to forget them. The shared name expresses their belonging to God.

relationship: close sensory blindness and deafness of Jacob's people
rationale: Isaiah describes a blind people and deaf people possessing ears; Jeremiah addresses Jacob and Judah as having eyes without seeing and ears without hearing. Both portray the community's failure of perception through the same sensory organs.

relationship: internal judicial challenge to announce and substantiate events
rationale: Isaiah 43 asks assembled nations for announcements and truthful witnesses; Isaiah 41 challenges the claimants to announce former and coming things so their claims to divinity can be tested. Both frame knowledge of events as evidence in the dispute.

relationship: parallel knowledge that the Lord is the only God
rationale: Isaiah appoints witnesses so they may know and believe God's identity and denies any other god before or after Him; Deuteronomy describes God's acts so Israel may know He is God and there is none beside Him.

relationship: related belief in 'I am' through disclosed events
rationale: Isaiah links witness, knowledge and belief with God's declaration 'I am'; Jesus says He tells events beforehand so that, when they happen, His hearers may believe 'I am.' The speakers and immediate disclosed events are distinguished.

relationship: close declaration of no Savior apart from the Lord
rationale: Both identify the speaker as the Lord God and expressly deny anyone who saves apart from Him. Hosea additionally recalls creation and the exodus.

relationship: related exclusive claim concerning salvation
rationale: Isaiah says no one saves apart from God; Peter names Jesus Christ and says salvation is in no one else and no other saving name is given. Acts makes its particular application to Jesus explicit.

relationship: related appointment of a people as witnesses
rationale: Isaiah's God calls the people witnesses to His announced and saving acts; Jesus tells His chosen apostles they will be His witnesses from Jerusalem to earth's end. Isaiah additionally declares God Himself a witness.

relationship: close impossibility of rescue from God's hand
rationale: Both explicitly deny that anyone can deliver or rescue from God's hands. Isaiah continues by asking who can reverse His action; Deuteronomy names His power to kill, make alive, strike and heal.

relationship: parallel Israel's Redeemer acting against Babylon
rationale: Isaiah's Redeemer promises intervention in Babylon for the people's sake; Jeremiah names their strong Redeemer and says He will judge His adversaries and provoke Babylon's inhabitants. The ships and fleeing in Isaiah are not repeated by Jeremiah.

relationship: historical counterpart of a path through the sea
rationale: Isaiah identifies the Lord as giving a way through sea and strong water; Exodus records His opening the sea so Israel crosses on dry ground. The narrative supplies the particular sea-passage pattern recalled by the description.

relationship: historical counterpart of the destruction of chariots and horsemen
rationale: Isaiah describes chariots, horse and mighty host brought out and finally extinguished; Exodus describes Pharaoh's horses, chariots and riders entering the sea and being covered, with none remaining. The sleep and wick metaphors are Isaiah's own images.

relationship: related movement of attention beyond former things
rationale: Isaiah commands not remembering or pondering former things before announcing a new divine work; Paul describes forgetting what is behind and stretching toward the goal ahead. The former things and the future object differ.

relationship: internal joining of wilderness water and a new road
rationale: Isaiah 43 promises a wilderness way and rivers in waterless land; Isaiah 35 likewise describes water bursting in wilderness, thirsty land becoming springs, and a Holy Way for the scattered.

relationship: parallel praise offered by wild creatures
rationale: Isaiah says wild beasts, sirens and ostrich daughters will bless God because He gives wilderness water; the psalm summons wild animals, cattle, creeping things and birds to praise His name. The species and the stated grounds differ.

relationship: close acquired people appointed to proclaim divine praise
rationale: Isaiah identifies God's acquired people as those who recount His praiseworthy deeds; First Peter likewise calls its addressees a people for God's possession so that they proclaim His excellences.

relationship: related divine denial of having burdened Israel
rationale: Isaiah's God says He did not make Israel toil; Micah's God asks how He grieved or troubled the people and recalls their redemption. This compares the labor clause without reversing Isaiah's opening statement that God did not call Jacob now.

relationship: related challenge concerning animal offerings as service to God
rationale: Isaiah says the sheep offerings were not for God and the sacrifices did not glorify Him; the psalm refuses supplied calves and goats, declares God's ownership of all animals and calls instead for a sacrifice of praise.

relationship: parallel rejection of God's supposed need for animal food
rationale: Isaiah says God did not desire the sacrifices' fat; the psalm says the world is His and asks whether He eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood. Both challenge the idea that sacrificial food meets a divine need.

relationship: close promise to forgive and no longer remember sins
rationale: Isaiah's God wipes out lawless acts and will not remember; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise likewise joins mercy toward injustices with sins remembered no more.

relationship: related confession of sins and restoration to right standing
rationale: Isaiah directs the addressee to state lawless acts so as to be justified; First John connects confession of sins with God's forgiveness and cleansing from unrighteousness. The stated outcomes are related but differently expressed.

relationship: parallel acknowledgment of ancestral lawlessness
rationale: Isaiah says the first fathers and their rulers acted lawlessly against God; the psalmist acknowledges sin with the fathers and recalls their failure to understand and remember God's deeds in Egypt. Isaiah does not specify that particular ancestral episode here.

relationship: historical counterpart of sanctuary defilement and national judgment
rationale: Isaiah links rulers defiling holy things with Jacob handed to destruction and Israel to reproach; Chronicles describes leaders, priests and people defiling the Lord's house, rejecting His messengers and being handed to the Chaldeans.

relationship: internal repeated naming of God's chosen servant
rationale: Both name Israel and Jacob as God's servant and chosen people. The recurring address identifies the people receiving the assurance without importing a different servant identity into this unit.

relationship: related divine formation from the womb and choice for service
rationale: Isaiah addresses chosen Jacob and Israel as formed from the womb; Jeremiah is told that God knew and consecrated him before his birth and appointed him a prophet. The corporate people and the individual prophet are distinct recipients.

relationship: close promise of God's Spirit upon descendants
rationale: Isaiah promises His Spirit upon the people's offspring and blessings upon their children; Joel promises an outpouring of His Spirit and prophecy by sons and daughters, extending also to male and female slaves.

relationship: related joining of thirst, water and the Spirit
rationale: Isaiah joins water for thirsty travelers with the Spirit placed upon offspring; Jesus invites thirsty people to drink, speaks of living water and, as John explains, means the Spirit believers will receive. John explicitly interprets its water image; Isaiah places the two promises alongside one another.

relationship: parallel flourishing through proximity to water
rationale: Isaiah compares the offspring's growth to grass amid water and a willow beside flowing water; the psalm compares the blessed person to a tree beside water outlets with fruit and an unfailing leaf. The plants and recipients differ within the shared growth image.

relationship: related confession of belonging to the Lord
rationale: Isaiah describes people declaring and inscribing that they belong to God in the names of Jacob and Israel; Zechariah describes the tested remnant answering God's 'My people' with 'The Lord is my God.' Both express acknowledged belonging, without matching the inscriptions.

relationship: internal declaration of divine priority and enduring existence
rationale: Isaiah 44 says God is first and after these things; Isaiah 48 says He is first and forever. Both assert His encompassing priority and continuance, preserving the supplied wording rather than replacing it with a standard first-and-last formula.

relationship: internal divine incomparability demonstrated by announcing events
rationale: Both deny a rival like God and connect His uniqueness with announcement of what is coming. Isaiah 44 challenges rivals to announce events before arrival; Isaiah 46 says He announces final things beforehand and His counsel stands.

relationship: internal witnesses to God's unique identity
rationale: Isaiah 44 asks the witnesses whether any God exists apart from Him and recalls His announcements; Isaiah 43 names the people witnesses to His announced and saving acts and denies other gods. This comparison concerns the witness and identity clauses.

relationship: parallel futility of hope in crafted gods
rationale: Isaiah calls image makers futile and their pleasing products unable to help; Wisdom calls hope in dead things wretched and identifies handmade objects called gods. Both expose the gap between craftsmanship and divine assistance.

relationship: parallel craftsman fashioning a futile god
rationale: Isaiah condemns fashioning a god and carving useless things; Wisdom describes a potter forming a futile god from the same clay used for ordinary vessels. The materials and crafts differ, while the manufactured deity's futility is explicit in both.

relationship: internal contrast of weakened maker and inexhaustible Creator
rationale: Isaiah's idol craftsman hungers and grows weak despite his strong arm; Isaiah 40 says God will not hunger or grow weary and gives strength to hungry people. The contrast separates the human maker's dependence from the Creator's sustaining power.

relationship: close wooden human image installed in a dwelling
rationale: Isaiah's woodworker shapes a human form and beauty to stand in a house; Wisdom's craftsman shapes leftover wood as a human image and prepares it a dwelling, setting and securing it in a wall. The technical details differ but the manufactured form and installation correspond.

relationship: parallel God growing and watering the trees
rationale: Isaiah says the wood came from woodland planted by the Lord and grown by rain; the psalm describes God watering mountains and trees filled, including the cedars He planted. Isaiah's subsequent idol manufacture thus uses a resource attributed to God.

relationship: close division of wood between cooking fuel and an image
rationale: Isaiah's people burn some wood for warmth and bread and make the rest into gods; Wisdom's craftsman burns scraps to prepare food and carves a remaining scrap as a human image. Both juxtapose ordinary fuel and a fabricated deity from the same material.

relationship: close burning of wood to prepare food and eat one's fill
rationale: Isaiah describes bread and roasted meat prepared over the wood, eaten to satisfaction; Wisdom likewise describes burned scraps used to prepare food and eating one's fill. Isaiah additionally supplies the warmth and the speaker's delighted exclamation.

relationship: related critique of expecting rescue from manufactured gods
rationale: Isaiah's maker worships the remaining wood and asks his carved god to rescue him; Jeremiah describes address to wood and stone, appeals for salvation in calamity, and challenges whether the manufactured gods can rise and save. The wording exposes dependence on what the people made.

relationship: close darkened understanding in the turn to images
rationale: Isaiah describes eyes and heart darkened from perception in the idol-making account; Paul describes futile thoughts and a darkened heart as people exchange divine glory for images of mortal beings. Paul develops the pattern as refusal to honor the known God.

relationship: parallel failure to reckon with an image's dependence
rationale: Isaiah rebukes failure to consider that wood used for cooking became a worshiped abomination; Wisdom likewise traces wood from food preparation to an installed image needing support, yet addressed in prayer. The accounts expose the irrational treatment of dependent material as a deity.

relationship: close heart-of-ashes description in idol criticism
rationale: Isaiah says their heart is ashes and they wander without rescue; Wisdom likewise calls the idol maker's heart ashes, his hope worthless and his life dishonorable because he failed to know his Maker. The shared image belongs to criticism of manufactured divinity in both contexts.

relationship: parallel command that Israel not forget its God
rationale: Isaiah reminds formed Jacob and Israel of servant status and commands Israel not to forget God; Deuteronomy warns not to forget the God who brought them from Egypt and commands service to Him. The direction of remembering is the people's duty in both.

relationship: close turning back connected with sins wiped away
rationale: Isaiah joins sins and lawless acts wiped away with the command to turn back to God and the promise of redemption; Peter likewise commands repentance and turning back so sins may be wiped away. The cloud and mist imagery belongs to Isaiah.

relationship: close cosmic rejoicing including heavens, earth and trees
rationale: Isaiah summons heaven, earth's foundations, mountains and trees to joy over God's mercy and redemption of Israel; the psalm summons heavens, earth and woodland trees to rejoice before God's coming judgment. The shared cosmic praise has distinct stated occasions.

relationship: close declaration that God alone stretched out heaven
rationale: Isaiah's God says He stretched heaven alone; Job likewise attributes stretching heaven to God alone. Both exclude a companion maker in this particular act, while their adjoining earth and sea descriptions differ.

relationship: parallel God making reputed wisdom foolish
rationale: Isaiah describes God turning the discerning backward and making their counsel foolish; Paul says God sets aside understanding and makes the world's wisdom foolish. Paul's quoted wisdom saying is not presented here as a direct quotation of Isaiah 44.

relationship: parallel promise of rebuilt Jerusalem and restored cities
rationale: Isaiah announces inhabited Jerusalem, rebuilt Judean cities and deserted places springing up; Zechariah announces God's compassionate return to Jerusalem, His house rebuilt and cities overflowing with good things. Both promise restored city life under God's action.

relationship: historical counterpart to God's drying of deep waters
rationale: Isaiah's God declares the abyss desolate and its rivers dry; the psalm recalls His rebuke drying the Red Sea and His guidance through the deep as wilderness. The psalm supplies a concrete past act corresponding to the divine authority over deep water.

relationship: historical counterpart of Cyrus commissioned for Jerusalem's temple
rationale: Isaiah names Cyrus, says he will do God's wishes and promises Jerusalem and the holy house's foundation; Ezra records God stirring Cyrus and the king's proclamation that God commissioned him to build His house in Jerusalem. Isaiah's actual instruction to Cyrus is to understand.

relationship: narrative counterpart of the temple foundation laid
rationale: Isaiah promises that God will lay the foundation of His holy house; Ezra records the builders laying the Lord's house's foundation and priests, Levites and people celebrating it. This connection focuses on the foundation itself rather than Cyrus's proclamation.
